title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Mastocytosis is a disorder characterized by mast cell accumulation, commonly in the skin, bone marrow, gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen, and lymphatic tissues. The World Health Organization divides cutaneous mastocytosis into 3 main categories. The first involves 3 or fewer lesions, called mastocytomas. The second involves between 4 and 100 lesions and is referred to as urticaria pigmentosa. The third category involves diffuse cutaneous involvement.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Urticaria pigmentosa is the most common form of cutaneous mastocytosis in children and can also present in adults. This condition is generally considered benign and self-resolving, often remitting in adolescence. Urticaria pigmentosa rarely involves internal organs, unlike adult forms of mastocytosis. However, complications may include the potential progression to a hematologic malignancy and mortality resulting from significant mast cell degranulation. Patients should be educated to avoid possible triggers and certain physical stimuli.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity reviews the characteristic clinical features of urticaria pigmentosa, distinctions from mimicking dermatologic and bullous disorders, and the rarity of internal organ involvement. Participants explore the World Health Organization classification of mastocytosis, with emphasis on the clinical spectrum of cutaneous disease. Learners gain greater diagnostic confidence, an enhanced ability to distinguish urticaria pigmentosa from similar conditions, and updated strategies for appropriate evaluation, counseling, and management. The activity also highlights the role of the interprofessional team in enhancing care delivery for affected patients across the lifespan.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Introduction
content: Mastocytosis is a disorder characterized by mast cell accumulation, commonly in the skin, bone marrow, gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen, and lymphatic tissues. The World Health Organization (WHO) categorizes mastocytosis into 3 main categories—cutaneous mastocytosis, systemic mastocytosis, and mast cell sarcoma. [1] The WHO then divides cutaneous mastocytosis into 3 main presentations. The first has solitary or few (≤3) lesions called mastocytomas. The second, urticaria pigmentosa, involves multiple, disseminated lesions. The number can vary widely, from less than 12 to more than 100 or even near-universal involvement. The last presentation involves diffuse cutaneous involvement.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Introduction
content: Urticaria pigmentosa is the most common form of cutaneous mastocytosis in children, but it can also occur in adults. This condition is considered benign and self-resolving, often remitting in adolescence. Internal organ involvement is rare in urticaria pigmentosa, unlike adult forms of mastocytosis. [2] What makes urticaria pigmentosa particularly distinctive is its tendency to manifest as small, itchy, reddish-brown, or yellowish-brown macules and papules, commonly referred to as urticaria or hives. These lesions typically appear in childhood and can persist throughout a person's life. The condition can vary in severity; although it is often benign, it may cause symptoms and complications related to mast cell activation. A thorough understanding of the clinical features, pathophysiology, and management of urticaria pigmentosa is critical for healthcare professionals to ensure accurate diagnosis and optimal patient care. [3]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Etiology
content: Urticaria pigmentosa is caused by several activating mutations in the KIT gene. When exposed to specific triggers, mast cells release mediators that cause the symptoms of mastocytosis. The released mediators are histamine, eicosanoids, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, heparin, proteases, and cytokines. Triggers include certain foods, exercise, heat, Hymenoptera and venomous stings, local trauma to skin lesions, alcohol, narcotics, salicylates, and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, polymyxin B, and anticholinergic medications. Some systemic anesthetic agents may induce anaphylaxis. [4]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Epidemiology
content: Mastocytosis can present at birth or develop at any time in late adulthood. This disorder occurs across all races and shows no gender bias. Although most patients do not have a family history of mastocytosis, familial cases have been reported. [5] Cutaneous mastocytomas occur in 15% to 50% of patients, urticaria pigmentosa in 45% to 75%, and diffuse cutaneous involvement in less than 5% to 10% of patients with mastocytosis. Most reported cases are in the Caucasian population. The cutaneous lesions of mastocytosis may be less visible in people with more heavily pigmented skin. The prevalence of autism spectrum disorders in children with mastocytosis was found to be 10 times higher than in the general population. [6]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Pathophysiology
content: Mast cell precursors express CD34, the tyrosine kinase receptor KIT (CD117), and immunoglobulin G receptors (Fc gamma RII). KIT can be activated by its ligand, stem cell factor, which induces mast cell growth and maturation and prevents apoptosis. Bone marrow stromal cells, keratinocytes, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and reproductive Sertoli and granulosa cells produce stem cell factor. The pathogenesis of mastocytosis is driven by multiple mutations in KIT , most commonly an activating mutation at codon 816, in which the amino acid aspartic acid (D) is substituted for valine (V, ie, D816V) or another amino acid. These amino acids result in constitutive ligand-independent activation of the receptor. Additional pathogenic factors remain to be investigated. [7] [8]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Pathophysiology
content: The increased concentrations of a soluble growth factor for mast cells in lesions of cutaneous mastocytosis are believed to stimulate mast cell proliferation, melanocyte induction, and melanin pigment production. The induction of melanocytes accounts for the hyperpigmentation commonly observed in cutaneous mast cell lesions. The pruritus observed in mastocytosis is associated with interleukin-31 production. [9] Impaired mast cell apoptosis has been postulated to be involved, as evidenced by the upregulation of the apoptosis-preventing protein BCL-2 demonstrated in the patients. [10] Interleukin-6 levels are elevated and correlated with disease severity, indicating its involvement in the pathophysiology of mastocytosis. [11]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Histopathology
content: Diagnosis of urticaria pigmentosa can be made clinically. However, a definitive diagnosis requires a skin biopsy. An anesthetic agent should be injected without epinephrine adjacent to, not directly into, the lesion chosen as the biopsy specimen to avoid mast cell degranulation, which makes histologic examination difficult.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Histopathology
content: The histological hallmark of urticaria pigmentosa is an increased density of mast cells in the dermis. Urticaria pigmentosa skin lesions can have a 40-fold increase in mast cell count relative to normal skin. [12] Mast cells have a rounded or cuboidal appearance (see Image. Mastocytosis). Mast cell nuclei are rounded with surrounding ample cytoplasm, producing a fried egg appearance. Typically, mast cells have a single nucleus; however, atypical histological findings have been reported in 4 patients with urticaria pigmentosa, showing mast cells with bilobed and multilobed morphology. [13] In nodular urticaria pigmentosa, mast cells are observed in dense aggregates and may extend through the entire dermis and into subcutaneous tissue.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Histopathology
content: If the lesion from which the biopsy specimen was taken was traumatized during harvest, edema and eosinophil infiltrates may be present. The hyperpigmentation of cutaneous mastocytosis results from increased melanin in the basal cell layer and melanophages in the upper dermis. Stains that help identify mast cells include toluidine blue, Leder, Giemsa, tryptase, and CD117 (KIT). Biopsy specimens from normal skin in patients with mastocytosis do not show increased mast cell numbers. Therefore, if there are no skin lesions and systemic mastocytosis is suspected, a bone marrow biopsy or a gastrointestinal tract biopsy may be indicated. A total serum tryptase level can help identify the extent of mast cell disease. A tryptase level >20 ng/mL represents one of the minor criteria for systemic mastocytosis. [14]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- History and Physical
content: Urticaria pigmentosa consists of small, monomorphic, tan- to brown-colored macules or papules distributed mainly on the trunk and typically spares the central face, palms, and soles (see Image. Urticaria Pigmentosa). This condition is similar to the lesions typically observed in adults. Lesions can be few or numerous and are about 1 to 2 cm in size; however, they can be larger. Darier's sign is the formation of a wheal upon stroking or rubbing skin lesions and suggests the diagnosis of cutaneous mastocytosis. The wheal forms due to the release of mast cell mediators, which can contribute to the systemic symptoms that may occur after stroking the lesion. Some lesions may blister upon stroking. Darier's sign is more pronounced in children than in adults due to an increased density of mast cells in their lesions. In approximately half of patients, stroking macroscopically uninvolved skin elicits dermographism. Large hemorrhagic bullous and infiltrative small vesicular variants may appear. Blistering predominates in infancy, whereas the grain-leather appearance of the skin and the pseudoxanthomatous presentation develop over time. Choudhary et al reported a patient with hyperpigmented lesions interspersed with normal skin, clinically suggestive of urticaria pigmentosa and a localized grain-leather plaque, typically observed in diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis. The extensive involvement of the body area suggests an unusual dual morphology. [15] There is a tendency to spare the scalp, face, palms, and soles; however, scarring alopecia has been documented. [16] Flushing may occur spontaneously after a cutaneous stroke or following the ingestion of a mast cell degranulating agent. Anaphylactic shock may occur.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- History and Physical
content: Systemic symptoms may include pruritus, abdominal pain, flushing, diarrhea, dizziness, palpitations, and syncope. Approximately 25% of patients with urticaria pigmentosa experience gastrointestinal symptoms. Complaints such as fever, malaise, night sweats, bone pain, epigastric distress, weight loss, and problems with cognitive disorganization often signal the presence of extracutaneous disease. Death can even occur from the extensive release of mast cell mediators. [17]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Evaluation
content: If the patient reports gastrointestinal symptoms, a barium study or endoscopy may be indicated. If a patient presents with bone pain or fractures, a radiographic skeletal survey or bone scan may be needed. Assessment for hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy is essential during examination. If an abnormality is suspected, a liver ultrasound or computed tomography scan should be ordered to investigate. If any of the tests show abnormal findings, a bone marrow biopsy should be considered. A complete blood count, serum tryptase level, liver function tests, and KIT gene analysis can be ordered. Tryptase levels may be more useful than histamine levels because histamine can be elevated in hypereosinophilic states. However, some consider it optional in the pediatric population. Unlike adults, children with cutaneous mastocytosis rarely have bone marrow involvement; hence, a biopsy is not advised. A reticular pigment network on a reddish background is characteristic of urticaria pigmentosa on dermoscopy. [18] Familiarity with the diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis is essential in the event of disease progression. [19]

content: The WHO criteria for systemic mastocytosis require meeting 1 major criterion and 1 minor criterion, or at least 3 minor criteria, as follows:

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Evaluation -- Major Criterion
content: Having multifocal, dense infiltrates of mast cells (aggregates ≥15 mast cells) in bone marrow or extracutaneous tissues
contents: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Evaluation -- Major Criterion. Having multifocal, dense infiltrates of mast cells (aggregates ≥15 mast cells) in bone marrow or extracutaneous tissues

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Evaluation -- Minor Criteria
content: More than 25% of mast cells in bone marrow samples or extracutaneous tissues are spindle-shaped or otherwise atypical Expression of CD25 and/or CD2 by extracutaneous mast cells (often determined using bone marrow flow cytometry) Presence of activating KIT codon 816 mutation in blood, bone marrow, or extracutaneous tissues Serum total tryptase level >20 ng/mL (chronically high serum tryptase is not a minor criterion if the patient has a hematologic malignancy)

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Evaluation
content: The criteria for diagnosing cutaneous mastocytosis are not well-defined. An international task group of experts from diverse organizations met on multiple occasions between 2010 and 2014 to establish criteria for cutaneous mastocytosis. [2] In patients with mastocytosis, macroscopically apparent characteristic skin lesions are the predominant criterion for cutaneous involvement. The task force suggests adding Darier's sign to this criterion. During Darier's sign evaluation, mastocytoma or nodular lesions in children might cause systemic reactions, including hypotension. Therefore, testing should be performed with caution in these patients. In all other cases, this approach should serve as the standard for diagnosing mastocytosis.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Evaluation
content: In addition to the primary criterion, 2 secondary criteria are typically observed, as delineated in the 2007 consensus. [20] The first criterion is histologic mast proliferation in lesional skin. Nevertheless, a definitive threshold for elevated mast cell counts has not been established. Some patients with cutaneous lesions have normal mast cell counts. This minor criterion remains valid, although pathologic findings may need to be correlated with clinical signs. In 2007, the second minor criterion was the presence of a KIT mutation in codon 816. Recent investigations indicate that 40% of pediatric patients have KIT mutations at additional codons. [21] The task force recommends renaming this criterion to (activating) the KIT mutation in lesional skin tissue. Nevertheless, it is essential to acknowledge that only a limited number of laboratories currently possess the capability to perform KIT gene sequencing on cutaneous tissue.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with cutaneous mastocytosis should avoid certain physical stimuli, including emotional stress, temperature extremes, physical exertion, bacterial toxins, envenomation by insects to which the patient is allergic, and rubbing, scratching, or traumatizing the lesions. Patients should also avoid potential triggers, including aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, codeine, morphine, alcohol, thiamine, quinine, opiates, gallamine, decamethonium, procaine, radiographic dyes, dextran, polymyxin B, scopolamine, and D-tubocurarine. [22] Crawfish, lobster, spicy foods, hot beverages, and cheese should be avoided. However, the role of the previously mentioned foods is hypothetical at this point and needs further investigation. [23] Using lukewarm water for bathing and air conditioning during hot weather is recommended. Treatment is mainly symptomatic for patients with cutaneous mastocytosis and includes the following:

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management
content: Topical medications that contain calcineurin inhibitors and corticosteroids (a potent class 1 topical corticosteroid, with occlusion if necessary) are used.
contents: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management. Topical medications that contain calcineurin inhibitors and corticosteroids (a potent class 1 topical corticosteroid, with occlusion if necessary) are used.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management
content: Intralesional injections of small amounts of dilute corticosteroids may temporarily or indefinitely resolve skin lesions. The risk of skin atrophy and adrenocortical suppression is minimized by treating only limited body areas during a single treatment session.
contents: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management. Intralesional injections of small amounts of dilute corticosteroids may temporarily or indefinitely resolve skin lesions. The risk of skin atrophy and adrenocortical suppression is minimized by treating only limited body areas during a single treatment session.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management
content: Systemic corticosteroids are useful only in specific situations, such as ascites, malabsorption, and severe skin disease. Case reports have described complete remission of bullous mastocytosis with oral corticosteroids, [24] but systemic therapy is often disappointing because the primary mechanism of action of corticosteroids is redistribution rather than mast cell death.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management
content: Systemic therapies, such as oral antihistamines (the mainstay of treatment), oral cromolyn sodium (specifically used for gastrointestinal symptoms), omalizumab, oral PUVA, narrowband ultraviolet B, and UVA1, can be used.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Treatment / Management
content: The use of the 585-nm flashlamp-pumped dye laser and the 532-nm neodymium:yttrium-aluminum-garnet (Nd:YAG) laser for the treatment of cutaneous mast cell lesions has been documented to yield cosmetic enhancement. [24] The pulsed dye laser at 595 nm is the most effective laser treatment for urticaria pigmentosa. [25]

content: A premeasured epinephrine pen with an autoinjector should be provided to all patients.

content: A successful case report described the treatment of progressive c- KIT mutation cutaneous mastocytosis with imatinib, halting disease symptoms and progression and improving the length of the disease course. [26] Masitinib may offer greater efficacy than sunitinib as a second-line treatment for patients with systemic or severe cutaneous mastocytosis that is resistant to imatinib. [27] In the future, patients' genetic profiles are likely to play a critical role in the development of tailored treatment strategies.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Bullous impetigo, secondary syphilis, carcinoid, leiomyoma, urticaria, juvenile xanthogranuloma, arthropod stings, and autoimmune bullous diseases are differential diagnoses. Increased mast cell numbers have been reported in other inflammatory and neoplastic skin conditions, including dermatofibromas, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and nevi. However, these disorders are also associated with additional characteristic histopathological changes in the skin that differ from those of mastocytosis. [28]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Prognosis
content: Prognostic indicators in cutaneous mastocytosis differ markedly between pediatric and adult cases, as well as among various mastocytosis subtypes, reflecting distinct underlying mechanisms and disease patterns. [29] The prognosis for childhood mastocytosis is excellent, with 50% to 70% of patients remitting before adolescence. Cutaneous mastocytosis onset after the age of 10 years portends a poorer prognosis because the late-onset disease tends to be persistent, is associated more often with systemic disease, and carries a higher risk of malignant transformation. [30]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Complications
content: Complications may include the possible transformation into a hematologic malignancy (mast cell leukemia) and death secondary to extensive mast cell degranulation. These potential outcomes underscore the importance of timely recognition and appropriate management.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence involves educating patients about potential triggers, such as specific foods, medications, insect stings, or physical stimuli, that can exacerbate their condition. By recognizing and avoiding these triggers, patients can mitigate symptom flare-ups and improve their overall quality of life. Simultaneously, patient education plays a vital role in helping individuals understand the nature of urticaria pigmentosa, emphasizing its typically benign course and the rarity of internal organ involvement.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients should also be educated about the importance of proper medication management, lifestyle modifications, and regular follow-up appointments. The significance of early intervention and regular medical check-ups to prevent complications associated with mast cell activation should be emphasized. Patients must be taught to recognize signs of systemic involvement and to seek prompt medical attention. Through a combination of deterrence strategies and comprehensive patient education, healthcare professionals empower individuals with urticaria pigmentosa to take an active role in managing their condition effectively and enhancing their well-being.

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Published studies suggest that children with mastocytosis have a higher rate of first-dose vaccine adverse effects than the overall population. These reactions are typically mild and temporary and do not occur after booster shots. Reactions mainly occur after hexavalent vaccines. Overall, children with mastocytosis should receive all required vaccines according to the recommended schedule. Single vaccines may reduce the risk of reactions more than polyvalent vaccines. [31]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Jarkvist et al determined that the overall incidence of food allergy reactions in patients with mast cell disorders is comparable to that observed in the general population, with the majority of responses being mild, nonallergic, and unconfirmed. In summary, there is no requirement for dietary restriction or elimination in the absence of a history of response to a suspected food. [32]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Proper skincare is essential, with an emphasis on preventing the skin from becoming excessively dry. Unscented creams with minimal components are advised. [31] Management of cutaneous mastocytosis necessitates a multidisciplinary approach, proper staging, and ongoing follow-up to identify potential complications. [29]

title: Urticaria Pigmentosa -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Healthcare professionals, including clinicians, advanced care practitioners, nurses, and pharmacists, need to develop the skills necessary for diagnosing and managing urticaria pigmentosa. These competencies include the ability to recognize characteristic skin lesions, differentiate them from other skin conditions, perform comprehensive patient assessments, and use appropriate diagnostic tests to confirm the diagnosis. Healthcare professionals should develop individualized treatment plans that incorporate medications, lifestyle modifications, and patient education to manage the condition effectively. Effective interprofessional communication is crucial in managing urticaria pigmentosa. Clinicians, nurses, pharmacists, and other healthcare providers must collaborate to ensure a holistic approach to care. Sharing information, insights, and treatment plans promotes optimal patient outcomes and safety. Timely and accurate information exchange and clear roles within the care team are essential for enhancing patient-centered care. This collaborative approach supports comprehensive care and improves the healthcare team's overall performance in treating patients with this unique skin disorder.
